    #10530. Midterm voters to decide on these key ballot measures, putting Trump’s agenda to the test

    A battle over abortion rights is playing out in several states Tuesday as voters decide 145 proposed laws and constitutional amendments, including some that could affect voting for future elections.

    The ballot measures provide a political undercard for a high-profile midterm election that will determine which party controls Congress, state legislatures and gubernatorial offices in many states.

    Some measures put President Donald Trump’s priorities to a public test by gauging support for his attempts to reshape congressional districts, limit transgender athletes in sports and strengthen voter identification requirements.

    Abortion ban faces an unusual redo in Missouri

    Two years ago, Missouri voters became the first in the nation to pass a ballot measure undoing an existing ban on most abortions.

    Now voters are deciding whether to repeal the 2024 abortion rights amendment and replace it with a new prohibition — this time allowing exceptions for medical emergencies and fetal anomalies, and in cases of rape or incest up to 12 weeks of pregnancy. The proposed ban was placed on the ballot by the Republican-led Legislature. Abortion rights advocates, led by national progressive groups, have greatly outspent abortion foes in a bid to defeat the measure.

    In three other states, ballot measures would create a right to abortion using standards similar to what was in place nationally before the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022 and opened the door to state bans.

    Ballot measures in Idaho and Nevada would block bans on abortion before fetal viability, usually considered after 21 weeks. Nevada voters already approved the measure once but have to do so a second time for it to become official. In Virginia, an amendment would ensure abortion is allowed for the first two trimesters.

    Redistricting measures could affect 2028 elections

    Nine states are using new congressional districts in the midterm elections after a rare spate of mid-decade redistricting encouraged by Trump.

    Missouri’s Republican lawmakers also had adopted new House districts designed to help the GOP win an additional seat. But courts ruled they cannot be used unless first approved by voters in a November referendum. If passed, the districts would take effect for the 2028 election.

    Voters in Democratic-led Maryland are deciding on a constitutional amendment that also could pave the way for new congressional districts in the 2028 election. Democratic proponents, backed by former President Barack Obama, have urged a “yes” vote as way to “stop Trump.”

    Some Democrats also want to redistrict in Colorado. But a citizen initiative on the ballot would prohibit any potential 2028 redistricting from favoring one political party and require approval from both an independent commission and the state Supreme Court.

    Transgender restrictions are proposed in several states

    Voters in Arizona, Colorado, Missouri, Nebraska and Washington are considering measures restricting transgender athletes or medical procedures. That comes as Trump’s administration has been pushing for restrictions impacting transgender people, especially youth.

    Most Republican-led states already bar transgender women and girls from female school sports teams. Citizen-led ballot initiatives propose similar restrictions in the Democratic-led states of Colorado and Washington. The Arizona measure would extend public school sports restrictions to private schools. And Nebraska’s measure would add existing restrictions to the state constitution.

    A second ballot question in Colorado would ban some transgender medical treatments for minors. The Missouri abortion amendment also would add existing transgender medical restrictions to the state constitution.

    Five state measures seek voter ID mandates

    Though Trump’s push for nationwide voter ID mandates remains stalled in Congress, citizen activists bypassed Democratic-led state legislatures to place new voter ID requirements on the ballot in California, Colorado and Nevada.

    Those measures would require government-issued identification — like driver’s licenses or partial Social Security numbers — to cast ballots. The Nevada amendment already won approval in 2024 but needs a second vote to take effect.

    Measures referred to the ballot by Republican-led legislatures in North Carolina and Ohio would enhance existing voter ID requirements by placing them in the state constitution.

    Six states consider citizen voting measures

    Ballot measures in Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Kansas, South Dakota and West Virginia would reinforce current election practices limiting voting to U.S. citizens.

    Critics argue the measures are largely symbolic and unnecessary, because voting by noncitizens is rare and already forbidden in federal elections. But noncitizens are allowed to vote in some local elections in California, Maryland, Vermont and the District of Columbia.

    Two years ago, similar citizen voting amendments won approval in all eight states where they appeared on ballots.

    Elections themselves are up for a vote in some states

    A Massachusetts ballot measure would end separate party primaries in favor of open primaries where the top two vote recipients of any party advance to the general election. In Alaska, voters are deciding for the second straight election whether to scrap their system of open primaries and ranked choice voting.

    Proposed amendments in North Dakota and South Dakota would make it harder to amend their state constitutions by requiring 60% approval from voters instead of a simple majority. A similar 60% threshold is proposed in Utah for citizen initiatives that raise taxes.

    Meanwhile, a Missouri amendment would make it harder for lawmakers to change voter-approved citizen initiatives by requiring revisions to get an 80% vote in the state House and Senate.

    Colorado amendment would aid immigration enforcement

    Trump’s immigration enforcement efforts could get a boost in Democratic-led Colorado under a proposed constitutional amendment that would chip away at state laws restricting cooperation with federal immigration agents.

    The proposed amendment, placed on the ballot by conservative activists, would require law enforcement officers to notify the U.S. Department of Homeland Security when someone with an illegal or unknown immigration status is charged with a violent crime or faces a new charge following a prior felony conviction.

    Arizona measure would limit traffic cameras

    Voters in Arizona are deciding on a proposal limiting the use of traffic cameras to catch drivers speeding or running red lights. The Republican-led Legislature referred the measure to voters after Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs vetoed a ban on the cameras.

    Hobbs said the cameras enhance roadway safety, but opponents contend they infringe on people’s privacy and point to instances of misuse by certain law enforcement officers.

    The proposal would bar new contracts for traffic camera systems starting in 2027 and require local governments to hold elections on whether to continue existing systems.

    About half the states, including Arizona, have communities that use cameras to enforce speeding or traffic signal laws, according to the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety.

    Associated Press writer Geoff Mulvihill contributed to this report.

    —David A. Lieb, Associated Press

    #10528. U.S. job postings rose sharply in September

    U.S. employers ramped up their job postings in September as stronger economic growth may be encouraging more hiring. Yet voters are headed to the polls Tuesday, largely gloomy over an economy beset by higher prices.

    U.S. job openings jumped to 7.5 million from a revised 7.19 million in August, the Labor Department reported Tuesday. It is the largest number of openings since May and up from a recent low of 6.9 million in March.

    The department’s Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) also showed that gross hiring—job gains before subtracting people who quit or lost jobs—rose and layoffs fell in September.

    The increases are a hopeful sign that hiring could improve, but the trend would have to continue for several months to suggest real progress. Hiring has been sluggish for nearly three years, though layoffs have also been historically low, a sign of meager “churn” in the labor market. Low churn means those who are employed are enjoying relatively high levels of job security, but it is much harder than normal for those looking for work to find a job.

    Still, the number of job openings now exceeds the number of unemployed, a sharp switch from a year ago when there were more people out of work than available jobs.

    “It’s an encouraging sign that despite all the headwinds right now with high diesel and gas prices and ongoing inflation problems, companies are slowly increasing their hiring,” Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, said.

    Job openings rose the most in professional and business services, which includes high-paying jobs in engineering and accounting, as well as jobs in the temp industry. Manufacturers, shipping firms, and state and local governments also advertised for more workers.

    Nicole Bachaud, a labor economist at ZipRecruiter, cautioned that with inflation still high and interest rates having increased since the summer, companies may not be able to ramp up hiring by much in the coming months.

    “All of that added up together just makes it much more expensive to operate as a business and much more expensive to expand,” she said. “And so that will likely continue to be a downward pressure on hiring, until we see inflation really able to cool down.”

    The government will issue the October jobs report on Friday, which is forecast to show that employers added 65,000 positions last month, according to data provider FactSet. That would be an improvement from 29,000 in September. The unemployment rate is expected to stay at a low 4.2%.

    Typically, job gains of just 65,000 would be seen as a sign of a struggling economy, but with the giant baby boom generation retiring and immigration sharply reduced, the economy doesn’t need to generate as many jobs as it has in the past for unemployment to remain low.

    In September, layoffs fell sharply to just 1.64 million, the fewest since March 2025. The number of people quitting their jobs rose to 3.37 million, the highest in about 18 months, and up from 3.04 million.

    The rise in quits is generally a good sign because workers usually leave a job when they either have another lined up or when they are confident they can find new work.

    —Christopher Rugaber, AP economics writer

    #10527. Election Day could mean big things for your 401(k). Here’s what history tells us

    Whether or not Tuesday’s midterm elections deliver a so-called blue wave, one thing is for certain: More volatility will likely ripple through financial markets.

    Midterm years have been historically weak for the U.S. stock market, delivering annual gains of just 7.5% versus an average return of 12.4% during non-midterm years, according to figures compiled by BlackRock. And even though more money has been pumped into this year’s midterm campaign than any other in history—to the tune of nearly $12 billion—your 401(k) portfolio isn’t likely to benefit so much.

    Despite polling that points to Democrats gaining seats, nay the majority, in Congress, investors haven’t been positioning for such an outcome. Rather, a survey of more than 100 institutional investors conducted by Wolfe Research suggests that these key market players haven’t positioned themselves for any particular result, according to CNBC.

    “Investors seem to have a significant dose of skepticism about whether the final outcome is going to be quite as favorable to Democrats as the polling suggests,” Tobin Marcus, the firm’s head of U.S. policy and politics, told the outlet. 

    Likewise, veteran market strategist Ed Yardeni warns that the stock market hasn’t fully priced in a blue wave, as such an outcome could lead to “much worse” partisanship in Washington, D.C. “It could be a very cold shower for the market in terms of the gridlock,” Yardeni, president of Yardeni Research, told Bloomberg. 

    WHY HISTORY FAVORS INVESTORS

    For long-term investors, the best course of action is ignoring the election results and staying invested. BlackRock cautions that “letting politics guide investment decisions has come at a significant cost” in recent years, as a $100,000 investment in the S&P 500 Index would have grown to nearly $400,000 at the start of this year, if left untouched, whereas investors who moved money out of the market in that timeframe based on their politics would have resulted in much lower returns. 

    What’s more, any kneejerk reaction to the election outcomes may not be as dire as some people are warning. 

    JPMorgan’s trading desk puts the odds of a Democratic sweep at 66%, which would lead to a rather tepid kneejerk immediate reaction for the S&P 500. Instead, the less-likely outcomes of Republicans retaining control of both the House and Senate (with odds of only 7%) or Democrats taking the House while Republicans maintain control of the Senate (with odds of 26%) could see stocks rise as much as 1.25%.

    And any dips or spikes in the stock market are likely to be short-lived. The S&P 500 has risen by an average of 14.1% in the six months following midterm elections since 1970, according to BlackRock, though scenarios where one party lost its majority control in the House and Senate—as polling suggests could happen this year—delivered returns of only 10.4% in that same period. 

    HOW THE OUTCOME COULD AFFECT INVESTORS

    Complicating matters for this particular midterm election is the surge in stocks this year that’s been fueled by unprecedented spending to support the AI buildout. Meanwhile, the Treasury market just suffered its worst quarterly selloff since 1994.

    That’s meant a mixed bag for retirement savers as the classic 60/40 portfolio has delivered lackluster results this year. This allocation model, popularized by the likes of famed investor John Bogle, is made up of 60% stocks and 40% bonds. So far this year, the classic 60/40 portfolio has delivered a return of nearly 7.1%, well below the 10.1% annualized return in the last 10 years, according to estimates by PortfoliosLab.

    A Democratic sweep of Congress could put more pressure on stocks—and particularly the high-flying AI stocks that have fueled most of the market’s rally this year. That’s because Democrats are seen as being more likely to pump the brakes on the data center projects that are crucial to the AI buildout and, hence, the market’s continued gains. 

    Because of how key the AI trade has become to the overall market, investors will closely watch a few key governor’s races—and particularly Texas, which Republican Governor Greg Abbott has called the “epicenter of AI development.” A surprise loss for the incumbent governor has the “potential to spook” the stock market in the short term, as Marcus told CNBC.

    On the other hand, if Republicans somehow manage to maintain control of both the House and Senate, it would have the most dramatic implications for the bond market, according to Reuters. That’s because the Republican policy agenda could continue, further expanding the deficit and therefore push Treasury yields even higher. 

    But no matter what happens, at the very least Wednesday will bring an end to the deluge of political advertisements and texts to voters—as well as the pre-election anxiety that can grip markets, as Ryan Detrick, chief market strategist at Carson Group, told CNBC. 

    “Once you are through it, it’s a big relief and markets tend to do pretty well.”

    #10526. The next big subscription service could be sunlight. And it might cost $5,000 an hour

    A satellite startup wants to fill the night sky with ultra-powerful beams of redirected sunlight. What could go wrong?

    According to astronomers, almost everything. Reflect Orbital’s plans to launch 50,000 satellites equipped with giant mirrors is akin to “a bullet in your head,” says one astrophysicist, citing threats to both the natural world and the future of astronomy.

    Selling the sun

    Reflect offers “sunlight-as-a-service,” planning to use its constellation of satellites to beam down five-kilometer-wide rays of sunlight on demand, ranging in brightness from “noon light to moon light.”

    Reflect’s website suggests potential use cases like powering solar panels, illuminating disaster zones and search-and-rescue missions, and lighting up worksites, cities, and events. But with a price tag of $5,000 for an hour of sunlight, the product would be prohibitively expensive for most customers—leaving critics to assume that only militaries and titans of industry are likely to make use of Reflect’s services, despite its altruistic branding.

    So far, Reflect hasn’t actually launched any satellites. In August, it received approval from the Federal Communications Commission to launch a single demonstration satellite (much to the chagrin of environmental groups, which urged the FCC to reverse its decision). But moving forward, Reflect won’t need to seek approval from the U.S. government at all: It recently purchased two space launches located in India, which will be liable for any unintended consequences of satellites launched from within its borders under the Outer Space Treaty.

    The end of astronomy

    The prospect of messing with the day-night cycle immediately raised conccerns with environmentalists and astronomers alike, who are already contending with an increasingly crowded night sky thanks to spacecraft like SpaceX’s fleet of Starlink satellites.

    Gaspar Bakos, an astrophysicist at Princeton University, told Sky & Telescope that Reflect’s plans for sunlight-on-demand are “essentially ignoring all the progress we have made for the past many decades in bringing awareness to and decreasing light pollution.”

    Bakos and other astronomers worry that the beams would cause light diffusion throughout the night sky, making it incredibly difficult for ground-based telescopes to view objects in space. Amateur astronomers would also be at risk of permanent eye damage if they happened to see one of Reflect’s beams through a telescope greater than 12 inches in aperture.

    Lighting up dark environments at night could also pose a threat to plants and animals that depend on the day-night cycle for biological regulation. That includes humans, whose own circadian rhythms dictate sleep patterns, hormones, and digestion among other bodily functions.

    Light bulb moment

    In an interview with Payload, Reflect CEO Ben Nowack responded to frequent concerns about his company’s plans. If astronomers are concerned about light pollution, Reflect will be sure to avoid getting in the way of their telescopes, he reasoned.

    “If there’s an astronomer or a place that doesn’t want to see light, and they have a really hard brightness requirement … we will make sure that we don’t serve customers close[by],” Nowack said.

    As for anxieties around the impact of life on Earth, Nowack chalks them up to a general fear of new technology.

    “Similar concerns and fears were brought up when light bulbs were introduced to the world, and people were worried about circadian rhythm and like, is this godly?” he said. 

    Never mind the fact that Reflect’s beams of sunlight would be just a touch brighter than light bulbs, casting light for up to 30 kilometers from their targets. Each satellite would also appear in the sky as a point source four magnitudes brighter than the moon, according to a report by Bakos and his colleagues.

    “This is not a ‘concern’—this is like a bullet in your head,” Bakos said. “It’s the end of ground-based astronomy.”

    #10523. Public Discord messages might start showing up in Google Search, unless users opt out

    Discord announced today that Discoverable Server web pages will begin showing summaries and pulled content, which might show up in search engines.

    Discord splits its servers into three different types: private, community, and discoverable. The latter is the most public version. No one needs an invite, and anyone can message, given that the admins of that server haven’t blocked you completely.

    In a recent press release, Discord notes that all Discoverable Servers will get a Server Web Page. The page is essentially an overall summary of that server, so users can easily gauge whether they its something they want to join.

    Discord says that discussion summaries will also appear on those server web pages, extracted from public channels. Any conversation that might be deemed noteworthy, whether by an AI model or moderator, could appear on that web page, and by extension, search engines like Google.

    It sounds like Discord is hoping channels surface in Google’s AI Mode or other engines, like Reddit, when users search for certain topics. It’s not a bad idea, as message boards often contain answers to incredibly niche questions otherwise hard to find on the internet.

    The release makes it clear that server admins can exclude certain channels and channel summaries, but doesn’t say the entire server can opt out. That seems to only be possible by switching server types.

    Discord says these changes will take effect starting November 16. Admins and users wishing to opt out of having their public messages and channels included in web pages, and by extension, search results, will need to opt out before then.

    #10521. RAMageddon is ready to rage on through 2030

    SK Hynix, one of the major companies behind memory production, says that it’s sold out through 2029, leaving RAMageddon ready to rage on for at least the next three years.

    On its latest earnings call today, SK Hynix confirmed that production of both DRAM and HBM (high-bandwidth memory) are effectively sold out not just for this year, not just for next year, but through 2029. That puts RAMageddon, the global shortage of memory, lasting at least another three years before we see any relief.

    SK Hynix’s CFO explains (via The Motley Fool, Seeking Alpha):

    …memory supply cannot keep pace with this level of demand growth, thus, we expect it to be difficult to fully meet customers’ volume requirements in the near term, given the complexities involved in implementing leading-edge processes and the lead times required to construct new production facilities. A situation where supply cannot keep up with demand is expected to persist for some time, a constraint projected to continue through 2030.

    Micron, one of the other companies responsible for memory production, previously said to expect 2027 to be “even tighter” compared to 2026.

    The SK Hynix call also details how the company is making long-term agreements which already account for “more than 50% of our total capacity for 2027 and 2028.”

    SK Hynix isn’t the biggest name in DRAM/HBM production, with Samsung accounting for a larger share, but everyone else is dealing with the same constraints. PCMag points out that SK Hynix is working to build out more production capacity, as everyone else is too, but it takes time to build out the complex infrastructure.

    Buckle up folks, this isn’t ending anytime soon. 🫠

    #10516. Amazon’s latest Echo smart displays and speakers reinforce Google Home’s lost lead

    Amazon just launched a new lineup of Echo smart speakers and a new smart display, all while Google Home’s lineup remains pretty quiet.

    Amazon has five new devices launching – two smart displays, a “Photo Frame,” and two speakers.

    Starting with the speakers, the latest Echo Dot has “a built-in smart home hub” and upgraded audio and starts shipping today for $100. Meanwhile, Echo Studio builds on that foundation with even-better audio and, optionally, a built-in camera. Those start at $220.

    On the smart display side, there’s the Echo Time, which is like an Echo Dot but with a small circular display built-in. Amazon touts “hundreds of clock faces” and “Omnisense” which can track your sleep just like Google’s second-gen Nest Hub, and it starts at $200.

    Echo Show 16, meanwhile, is a big 16-inch smart display meant to live on your wall with support for smart home controls, the ability to show a family calendar, and full Fire TV built-in as well. It starts at $500 and, like everything else mentioned so far, is built around Amazon’s AI-enhanced Alexa.

    Rounding out the lineup is the Alexa Photo Frame, a simpler smart display that has Alexa built-in but focuses on showing photos from your Amazon Photos library. It has a 10-inch anti-glare display and a design that looks like a normal photo frame and starts at $200.

    Google Home really is just so wildly behind isn’t it.

    In looking at Amazon’s lineup, I can’t help but feel like Google is just wasting potential here. A smart speaker that doubles as a Nest Cam would be awesome. The same goes for a giant Nest Hub that doubles as a Google TV.

    I still don't understand how nobody is questioning Google when they still don't support basics stuff like:

    casting from the phone using a "video" app (YouTube, Netflix, etc) to Google Cast speakers -> AirPlay has supported this for a decade

    being able to set Google Cast speakers as audio output devices of Google TV devices (and not the extremely limited - and frankly, basically useless - implementation that there's only between Google TV Streamer and the new Google Home Speaker) -> both Amazon and Apple (as well as many competitors) have supported this for several years, including with with surround setups (4 speakers)

    Their latest Google Home Speaker was a major disappointment. I almost have no doubt that a new Google Home Hub and a new Google TV Streamer will be disappointments too.

    It's years that I keep wishing for Google to prove me wrong, but all they do is keep digging themselves deeper in their grave.

    And, seriously, how does Google not sell (or at least partner with someone) a Google Photos digital photo frame. Google Photos is a wildly successful platform and that would sell like hotcakes. Big “how am I not in that movie” energy.

    I’ve said it before, but Google Home had such a lead in the smart speaker and smart display market, especially with Google’s ecosystem tie-ins, but Amazon is currently running laps around it with products that Google should be selling. Throw in that even Apple has a smart display now where Google hasn’t even teased a new Nest Hub, and it just feels all kinds of bad to be in Google’s camp right now.

    #10509. Building Location-Aware Interfaces Without Mixing Up Language, Currency, and Region

    Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

    Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

    Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

    A visitor opens an online store while traveling. Their browser uses English, their account is registered in Canada, their network appears to be in Germany, and their delivery address is in France.

    Which currency should the store show? Which products are available? What language should the checkout use?

    There is no single answer hidden inside a country code. These decisions depend on different signals and different product rules.

    For developers and designers, the challenge is to represent that context explicitly. Otherwise, a convenient shortcut—such as deriving everything from an IP address—can produce confusing prices, unexpected redirects, and incorrect availability.

    This article walks through a practical approach to building a regional product interface, with examples that also apply to travel sites, service directories, and applications that retrieve current web information.

    Avoid a single variable named country that silently controls every aspect of the interface.

    These values can disagree without any of them being wrong.

    For an anonymous visitor, network region might help suggest an initial market. Once the user selects a destination, the application should not silently replace it because a later request arrives from a different network.

    Write precedence rules for each decision. Language selection and delivery eligibility need separate policies.

    SitePoint’s introduction to JavaScript internationalization provides useful background on separating software capabilities from locale-specific adaptation.

    This is an illustrative application contract. It keeps the observation's market, currency, and timestamp attached to the value.

    Without that context, another component might reuse the amount for a different market or label it as current long after availability changes.

    At the API boundary, validate the required fields and their allowed values. A missing amount must not become zero, and a missing availability value must not become “in stock.”

    Also define the timestamp precisely. Does it mean the source was fetched, the source published an update, or your database last processed the record? Those are different events.

    For the interface, use wording consistent with the evidence: “Checked at 09:00” is more precise than “Live availability” when you only have a timestamped observation.

    Browser preferences and network location operate at different layers.

    Changing the browser locale can affect language preferences and formatting. It does not relocate the connection seen by the server. Similarly, supplying browser geolocation coordinates does not change the network's public IP address.

    This distinction also matters in live-web retrieval. Bixberry describes an opt-in network that routes requests through participants' internet connections. It illustrates how retrieval infrastructure can involve connections outside a conventional data-center environment.

    When comparing two responses, record the relevant conditions:

    Keep diagnostic records minimal and avoid retaining unnecessary personal information.

    For authorized regional testing of your own application, SitePoint’s guide to testing geo-dependent web apps offers related background on separating browser settings from network behavior.

    JavaScript's Intl.NumberFormat formats numeric values according to locale and currency settings:

    Both calls represent the same euro amount. Formatting it for a different locale does not convert it to another currency.

    Do not turn a euro price into a dollar price by changing only the currency argument. A conversion requires a defined exchange-rate source, timestamp, rounding policy, and explanation of whether the result is an estimate or the actual charged amount.

    For calculations, choose a representation appropriate to your pricing model rather than relying on floating-point arithmetic throughout. If using integer minor units, remember that currencies do not all use two decimal places.

    SitePoint’s overview of the JavaScript Internationalization API explains related formatting capabilities.

    Practical check: switch interface language while leaving the selected market unchanged. The number format may change, but the underlying price and currency should remain consistent with the product rules.

    A country flag is a weak substitute for a language label. Countries can have multiple languages, and the same language can be used across many countries.

    Use clear, separate controls when the product needs them:

    Do not expose a control unless its effect is meaningful and implemented consistently. A currency selector that updates a price label but leaves checkout charging behavior unexplained creates confusion.

    Before a market change, explain consequential effects. For example:

    Changing your delivery country may update availability and delivery options.

    Preserve the user's task where possible. If a product is unavailable in the newly selected market, retain its page and show an explanation instead of sending the user to an unrelated homepage.

    For designers, test longer translations, currency codes, and expanded validation messages. Use logical CSS properties where appropriate so layouts can adapt to right-to-left content:

    These rules are a starting point, not a complete localization solution. Review reading order, icons, numeric content, and translated copy with people familiar with the target language.

    A regional interface can behave correctly at the origin and still show incorrect content when a shared cache serves the wrong variant.

    If a response varies by market or language, that variation must be reflected in your cache design. One option for public content is an explicit route structure:

    These routes are illustrative. They make market and language differences visible, but the rest of the cache configuration must still match the application's behavior.

    Personalized prices and account-specific responses require their own cache policy. A public page cache must not expose one account's content to another.

    Test the deployed caching layer, not only a local development server:

    Keep freshness requirements separate from variant separation. A response can belong to the correct market and still be too old.

    Playwright's emulation settings let tests configure locale, time zone, geolocation, and permissions.

    This assumes a configured base URL and an application implementing the illustrated route and selectors. It tests the application's handling of explicit market selection under a different locale; it does not prove that the request originated in Germany.

    Use controlled API fixtures for predictable frontend tests, then test real routing and caching separately. Browser emulation is one layer of verification, not a substitute for every regional check.

    A location-aware application should be able to explain why it chose a language, price, destination, or availability result.

    Keep those decisions separate, preserve the context of retrieved data, and make explicit user choices easy to change. Then test the situations where signals disagree.

    The result is an interface that works for travelers, multilingual households, remote workers, and anyone whose preferences cannot be reduced to the location of their current internet connection.

    As I opened the NBA app on XREAL Aura and tapped the tabletop option, I watched the coffee table in front of me transform into a basketball court, complete with models of each player moving around the court in real-time. It was as if I were a giant looking in through the top of the arena. Not only could I get as close or as far away as I wanted, but all the game’s important stats were right there for me to peruse. The video below is taken from the Apple Vision Pro, but the experience is similar on XREAL Aura.

    It was one of the most convincing reasons I’ve seen to own a pair of legit smart glasses, and the very reason XREAL chose to launch with Google’s Android XR at its core. All your favorite Android apps are here and work exactly as you hoped, and a curated selection of 150 now delivers a real sense of presence to the heart and soul of each app’s experience.

    But it’s not just about compatibility or interoperability, either. The reach of Google’s Android platform means that big names like NBA, NASCAR, the San Francisco Ballet Company, Hulu, Netflix, Disney+, and so many more are playable in-glasses on day one, many with bespoke XR experiences.

    Acclaimed actor and director Andy Serkis is even in on the mix with Nevatars, an Android XR exclusive that follows a character artist’s abandoned digital creations and will be free for the first 6 months. And then there’s Asteroid, a new type of immersive film from Doug Liman that takes the cinematic storytelling of a movie and meshes it with interactive gameplay via live conversational AI (Gemini). This one’s exclusive to Android XR and free for XREAL Aura owners.

    Some of the most popular VR developers are also on board, including Resolution Games, who returns with a fresh port of the D&D-like strategy game, Demeo, plus the Android XR-exclusive Holochess (which is already on the Play Store). Holochess transforms the normally turn-based chess rules into a real-time strategy battle of Clankers vs. Xenoswarm, all on the table right in front of you. This 2-player game is free-to-play, and a third faction can be unlocked for $2.99.

    There are also a ton of spatial games and experiences to play, as well as. Simply Piano XR merges physical instruments with virtual ones, giving you a real-time way to learn and improve your music skills while wearing your glasses. And that’s just the tip of the iceberg as developers continue to branch out with new, creative ways of using spatial computing devices like XREAL Aura.

    #10506. Supercharge your OCR Pipelines with Open Models

    We have added Chandra and OlmOCR-2 to this blog, as well as OlmOCR Scores of the models 🫡

    By the end, you’ll know how to choose the right OCR model, start building with it, and gain deeper insights into document AI. Let’s go!

    Optical Character Recognition (OCR) is one of the earliest and longest running challenges in computer vision. Many of AI’s first practical applications focused on turning printed text into digital form.

    With the surge of vision-language models (VLMs), OCR has advanced significantly. Recently, many OCR models have been developed by fine-tuning existing VLMs. But today’s capabilities extend far beyond OCR: you can retrieve documents by query or answer questions about them directly. Thanks to stronger vision features, these models can also handle low-quality scans, interpret complex elements like tables, charts, and images, and fuse text with visuals to answer open-ended questions across documents.

    Recent models transcribe texts into a machine-readable format.The input can include:

    OCR models convert them into machine-readable text that comes in many different formats like HTML, Markdown and more.

    On top of text, some models can also recognize:

    Some models know where images are inside the document, extract their coordinates, and insert them appropriately between texts. Other models generate captions for images and insert them where they appear. This is especially useful if you are feeding the machine-readable output into an LLM. Example models are OlmOCR by AllenAI, or PaddleOCR-VL by PaddlePaddle.

    Models use different machine-readable output formats, such as DocTags, HTML or Markdown (explained in the next section Output Formats). The way a model handles tables and charts often depends on the output format they are using. Some models treat charts like images: they are kept as is. Other models convert charts into markdown tables or JSON, e.g., a bar chart can be converted as follows.

    Similarly for tables, cells are converted into a machine-readable format while retaining context from headings and columns.

    Different OCR models have different output formats. Briefly, here are the common output formats used by modern models.DocTag: DocTag is an XML-like format for documents that expresses location, text format, component-level information, and more. Below is an illustration of a paper parsed into DocTags. This format is employed by the open Docling models.

    The right model depends on how you plan to use its outputs:

    Documents can have complex structures, like multi-column text blocks and floating figures. Older OCR models handled these documents by detecting words and then the layout of pages manually in post-processing to have the text rendered in reading order, which is brittle. Modern OCR models, on the other hand, incorporate layout metadata to help preserve reading order and accuracy. This metadata is called “anchor”, it can come in bounding boxes. This process is also called as “grounding/anchoring” because it helps with reducing hallucination.

    OCR models can either take in images and an optional text prompt, this depends on the model architecture and the pre-training setup.Some OCR models support prompt-based task switching, e.g. granite-docling can parse an entire page with the prompt “Convert this page to Docling” while it can also take prompts like “Convert this formula to LaTeX” along with a page full of formulas.Other models, however, are trained only for parsing entire pages, and they are conditioned to do this through a system prompt.For instance, OlmOCR by AllenAI takes a long conditioning prompt. Like many others, OlmOCR is technically an OCR fine-tuned version of a VLM (Qwen2.5VL in this case), so you can prompt for other tasks, but its performance will not be on par with the OCR capabilities.

    We’ve seen an incredible wave of new models this past year. Because so much work is happening in the open, these players build on and benefit from each other’s work. A great example is AllenAI’s release of OlmOCR, which not only released a model but also the dataset used to train it. With these, others can build upon them in new directions. The field is incredibly active, but it’s not always obvious which model to use.

    To make things a bit easier, we’re putting together a non-exhaustive comparison of some of our current favorite models. All of the models below are layout-aware and can parse tables, charts, and math equations. The full list of languages each model supports are detailed in their model cards, so make sure to check them if you’re interested. All models below have open-source license except for Chandra having OpenRAIL license and Nanonets license being unclear. The average scores are taken from model cards of Chandra, OlmOCR, evaluated on OlmOCR Benchmark, which is English-only. Many of the models in this collection have been fine-tuned from Qwen2.5-VL or Qwen3-VL, so we also provide Qwen3-VL model below as well.

    While Qwen3-VL itself is a powerful and versatile vision-language model post-trained for document understanding and other tasks, it isn’t optimized for a single, universal OCR prompt. In contrast, the other models were fine-tuned using one or a few fixed prompts specifically designed for OCR tasks. So to use Qwen3-VL, we recommend experimenting with prompts.

    Here’s a small demo for you to try some of the latest models and compare their outputs.

    There’s no single best model, as every problem has different needs. Should tables be rendered in Markdown or HTML? Which elements should we extract? How should we quantify text accuracy and error rates? 👀While there are many evaluation datasets and tools, many don’t answer these questions. So we suggest using the following benchmarks:

    When testing different OCR models, we've found that the performance across different document types, languages, etc., varies a lot. Your domain may not be well represented in existing benchmarks! To make effective use of this new generation of VLM-based OCR models we suggest aiming to collect a dataset of representative examples of your task domain and testing a few different models to compare their performance.

    Most OCR models are small, having between 3B and 7B parameters; you can even find models with fewer than 1B parameters, like PaddleOCR-VL. However, the cost also depends on the availability of optimized implementations for specialized inference frameworks. For example, OlmOCR-2 comes with vLLM and SGLang implementations, and the cost per million pages is 178 dollars (assuming on H100 for $2.69/hour). DeepSeek-OCR can process 200k+ pages per day on a single A100 with 40GB VRAM. With napkin math, we see that the cost per million pages is more or less similar to OlmOCR (although it depends on your A100 provider). If your use case remains unaffected, you can also opt for quantized versions of the models. The cost of running open-source models heavily depends on the hourly cost of the instance and the optimizations the model includes, but it’s guaranteed to be cheaper than many closed-source models out there on a larger scale.

    While the past year has seen a surge in open OCR models, this hasn't been matched by as many open training and evaluation datasets. An exception is AllenAI's olmOCR-mix-0225, which has been used to train at least 72 models on the Hub – likely more, since not all models document their training data.

    Sharing more datasets could unlock even greater advances in open OCR models. There are several promising approaches for creating these datasets:

    It's worth noting that many such datasets exist but remain unused. Making them more readily available as 'training-ready' datasets carries a considerable potential for the open-source community.

    We have received many questions about getting started with OCR models, so here are a few ways you can use local inference tools and host remotely with Hugging Face.

    Most cutting-edge models come with vLLM support and transformers implementation. You can get more info about how to serve each from the models’ own cards. For convenience, we show how to infer locally using vLLM here. The code below can differ from model to model, but for most models it looks like the following.

    And then you can query as follows using e.g. OpenAI client.

    Transformers provides standard model definitions for easy inference and fine-tuning. Models available in transformers come with either official transformers implementation (model definitions within the library) or “remote code” implementations. Latter is defined by the model owners to enable easy loading of models into transformers interface, so you don’t have to go through the model implementation. Below is an example loading Nanonets model using transformers implementation.

    MLXMLX is an open-source machine learning framework for Apple Silicon. MLX-VLM is built on top of MLX to serve vision language models easily. You can explore all the OCR models available in MLX format here. They also come in quantized versions.You can install MLX-VLM as follows.

    Inference Endpoints for Managed DeploymentYou can deploy OCR models compatible with vLLM or SGLang on Hugging Face Inference Endpoints, either from a model repository “Deploy” option or directly through Inference Endpoints interface. Inference Endpoints serve the cutting-edge models in a fully managed environment with GPU acceleration, auto-scaling, and monitoring without manually managing the infrastructure.

    Here is a simple method of deploying nanonets using vLLM as the inference engine.

    For many OCR applications, you want to do efficient batch inference, i.e., running a model across thousands of images as cheaply and efficiently as possible. A good approach is to use vLLM's offline inference mode. As discussed above, many recent VLM-based OCR models are supported by vLLM, which efficiently batches images and generates OCR outputs at scale.

    To make this even easier, we've created uv-scripts/ocr, a collection of ready-to-run OCR scripts that work with Hugging Face Jobs. These scripts let you run OCR on any dataset without needing your own GPU. Simply point the script at your input dataset, and it will:

    The scripts handle all the vLLM configuration and batching automatically, making batch OCR accessible without infrastructure setup.

    If you are interested in document AI, not just OCR, here are some of our recommendations.

    Visual document retrieval is to retrieve the most relevant top-k documents when given a text query. If you have previously worked with retriever models, the difference is that you search directly on a stack of PDFs. Aside from using them standalone, you can also build multimodal RAG pipelines by combining them with a vision language model (find how to do so here). You can find all of them on Hugging Face Hub.

    There are two types of visual document retrievers, single-vector and multi-vector models. Single-vector models are more memory efficient and less performant; meanwhile, multi-vector models are more memory hungry and more performant. Most of these models often come with vLLM and transformers integrations, so you can index documents using them and then do a search easily using a vector DB.

    If you have a task at hand that only requires answering questions based on documents, you can use some of the vision language models that had document tasks in their training tasks. We’ve observed users trying to convert documents into text and passing the output to LLMs, but if your document has a complex layout, and your converted document outputs charts and so on in HTML, or images are captioned incorrectly, the LLM will miss out. Instead, feed your document and query to one of the advanced vision language models like Qwen3-VL not to miss out on any context.

    In this blog post, we wanted to give you an overview of how to pick your OCR model, existing cutting-edge models and capabilities, and the tools to get you started with OCR.If you want to learn more about OCR and vision language models, we encourage you to read the resources below.

Pikmin series of shorts.

    Players will be able to use the Switch 2’s built-in microphone to issue voice commands to Oatchi, the space dog. The series will then debut one short per month starting in December. The shorts build on the success of Close to You, a Pikmin animation released last year.

    #10504. New Zelda and GTA represent a games industry that no longer exists

    The two biggest games of the year launch in November, offering some reprieve from a terrible year.﻿

    The two biggest games of the year launch in November, offering some reprieve from a terrible year.﻿

    Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

    Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

    The two biggest games of 2026 are set to launch just a few weeks apart in November.

    On the one side you have the behemoth that is Grand Theft Auto VI, an experience 13 years in the making, and the sequel to one of the best-selling games in history. Its predecessor, GTA V, has sold a staggering 230 million copies since it launched in 2013, and was re-released across three generations of consoles. Developer Rockstar is a pioneer in the realm of open-world games, dating back to GTA III, and the scale and ambitions of those worlds have steadily grown since then. With GTA V and later Red Dead Redemption 2, the studio’s ideas reached a new level of realism. And the sixth GTA looks poised to eclipse them both, which has created an unprecedented level of demand.

    Analyst firm Circana estimates that 29 percent of gamers in the US intend to buy the game, with demand so large it could boost flagging console sales. “Many consumers who have yet to upgrade to a current-generation console may choose to purchase a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series specifically to play the title,” analyst Mat Piscatella says in a statement. GTA VI’s reach is so vast that almost every other major game launched early to avoid it.

    The one exception is Nintendo. The company’s tentpole release for the holidays, and its next major exclusive for the Switch 2, is a lavish remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

    The release is notable for a few reasons. For one thing, it’s an attempt from Nintendo to modernize one of the most influential and beloved games in its long history. The original Ocarina of Time was the world’s first introduction to a 3D iteration of Hyrule, which, in turn, made it an early glimpse at what was possible in three-dimensional spaces, laying a blueprint for countless games that came afterward. Nintendo has since expanded on that, turning Switch-era adventures Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom into wide-open adventures designed for player creativity. They went on to become some of the best-selling games for Nintendo’s most successful console.

    Ocarina of Time’s launch also comes just ahead of a live-action Zelda movie in 2027, which could catapult the franchise to a new level of prominence. That’s why Nintendo is seemingly the only company unafraid of competing with GTA.

    These aren’t just two blockbuster games – they’re two series with the pull to make this a real cultural moment, akin to “Barbenheimer” but for video games. They’re the kind of launches that make it onto Saturday Night Live and have NBA players worried.

    It’s just too bad about the rest of the industry.

    These major November releases are something of a mirage, two outliers that stand out amid the wreckage that is the rest of the video game industry. While there have been plenty of major releases and great games this year, the main theme of 2026 has been just how dire things have become. Layoffs, studio closures, unpopular business models, the ever-looming threat of AI, and massive increases in hardware costs have combined to create an ominous cloud over the medium.

    Here is just a snapshot of what the year has been like: Xbox is in the middle of a “reset” that involves laying off thousands of developers, shutting down some studios, and gutting others; Fortnite developer Epic cut more than 1,000 jobs due to a sharp downturn in the live-service games space, and it’s currently going all-in on vibe coding; Sony is also struggling, slashing jobs at Destiny developer Bungie, watching console sales plummet as costs skyrocket, and raising the ire of gamers by moving on from physical media; and meanwhile, major publishers like EA and Ubisoft are in their own dramatic states of upheaval.

    And the bad news hasn’t really let up. Just last week, EA shut down beloved studio BioWare and canceled the next Mass Effect game, and this week Sony studio Sucker Punch cut staff despite the success of last year’s Ghost of Yōtei. Every day, it seems, brings some new unwelcome development.

    Clearly, things are changing for the video game industry; they have to change. What that future looks like, though, remains unclear. The next generation of game consoles is being threatened by exorbitant prices, and all the while the rise of AI-powered tools is sending ripples across the industry, threatening the established order between players and creators as games are ported to every platform imaginable. “These are unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when (and sometimes because) they challenge our existing business models,” Xbox CEO Asha Sharma said in a recent memo. But how that plays out remains to be seen.

    It’s not all doom and gloom. There have been rare success stories, where studios like FromSoftware and Remedy have managed to carve out a sustainable existence in a turbulent field. But for the most part, the established norms that have been part of the blockbuster games industry for years are going away. Big games are too expensive to make, hardware is too expensive to buy (and the cost is only going up), and somewhere, something has to give.

    It’s tempting to look at Zelda and GTA as answers to these problems. After all, if Nintendo and Rockstar are doing so well, there must be a solution out there. But they’re also two very specific cases that are essentially impossible to replicate. Nintendo maintains ownership over all aspects of its platform, from the hardware to the games, and it has taken a careful and largely risk-averse approach that has allowed it to weather the current storm and create a growing entertainment empire. Rockstar, meanwhile, is the rare example of being too big to fail. GTA V was so massive for so long — Circana says it was among the top 20 best-selling games in the US for 13 straight years — that it allowed the studio to build up both an unprecedented amount of anticipation and, it seems, a game big enough to match it.

    In that way, Zelda and GTA are throwbacks to a time when major games were sure bets. Their duelling releases are fascinating both because these games are so impactful, but also because, with all of the impending upheaval, the industry might never see a moment like this again.

    #10503. 10 Software Security Practices Built for the Next 250 Years

    This Cybersecurity Awareness Month's theme, "Securing the Next 250," asks us to look beyond vulnerabilities and consider what will make our digital systems resilient for generations.

    When I testified before Congress with my L0pht colleagues in 1998, we warned that insecure software could put the systems society depended on at risk. Technology has changed dramatically since then, but the fundamental security questions remain familiar. Where does untrusted data enter? What authority does a component have? Who owns the risk, and how do we know a control worked?

    We cannot predict the technology stack of 2276, but we can establish practices that make software trustworthy as technology evolves. These 10 are a good place to start.

    Make security part of the architecture. Secure by design should describe how a system is engineered, beginning with secure defaults, approved patterns, clear trust boundaries, and controls that make insecure outcomes difficult. When security is introduced near the end of development, it must work against decisions already embedded in the architecture, while built-in controls become part of how the system operates and evolves.

    Maintain an accurate picture of what you have. Every organization needs a continuously updated inventory of its applications, open source dependencies, development tools, AI models, and external services, along with clear ownership for critical systems. When a serious vulnerability emerges, teams should be able to determine quickly where the affected component is running, what it can reach, and who is responsible for addressing it.

    Verify every line of code. Code should earn trust whether it was written by an employee, generated by an AI assistant, or obtained from a third party. Our research found that 44% of AI-generated coding tasks introduced a known vulnerability, which means organizations adopting these tools need independent security testing that operates at the same speed as development and verifies code before it reaches production.

    Make the secure path the easiest path. Developers work under constant pressure to ship, so security controls that produce excessive noise, delay builds, or pull people away from their normal tools will eventually be bypassed. Organizations should put precise feedback, approved components, and validated fixes directly into repositories, pipelines, and coding workflows, making the secure approach the most efficient way to complete the work.

    Match security speed to development speed. AI is turning software insecurity into a throughput problem because teams can now produce and change code faster than manual review can follow. Testing, policy enforcement, and remediation therefore need to operate continuously across the development life cycle, with automation handling repeatable work and people concentrating on the complex decisions that require business context and judgment.

    Control what enters the software supply chain. Modern applications are assembled from large volumes of code that organizations did not write, and each dependency introduces another relationship that must be understood and maintained. Teams should evaluate components when they enter a build, record their provenance, detect malicious or abandoned packages, and plan for safe upgrades, since an inventory alone cannot prevent risky software from being introduced.

    Pay down security debt before it comes due. Veracode's research found that security debt now affects 82% of organizations, leaving an expanding reservoir of vulnerabilities that have remained unresolved for more than a year. As AI-powered discovery compresses years of vulnerability research into months, leaders need to fund remediation as an ongoing engineering function, define expectations for addressing the highest-risk flaws, and track whether new risk is accumulating faster than teams can remove it.

    Measure the risk you remove. Most security programs can report how many vulnerabilities they found and closed, yet those activity measures do not show whether the organization has become safer. More useful measures include how long critical, exploitable flaws remain exposed, whether fix capacity is keeping pace with incoming risk and how quickly teams can reduce exposure in applications tied to sensitive data or essential business operations.

    Threat-model the entire AI system. An AI agent includes far more than the model because its identity, permissions, tools, memory, data, runtime, and network access all contribute to what it can ultimately do. Organizations should authorize sensitive actions where they occur, constrain what compromised components can reach, include the runtime in data-flow analysis, and retain enough evidence to determine what the agent did when something goes wrong.

    Preserve human accountability. Every important application and accepted risk needs an accountable owner, supported by evidence of the controls applied, tests performed, and decisions made throughout the software life cycle. As machines assume a larger role in writing and modifying code, people must retain enough understanding to challenge the output, recognize unexpected behavior, and demonstrate that reasonable precautions were taken.

    Related:One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

    The next 250 years will bring technologies that we cannot name today, although the systems built with them will still have inputs, privileges, dependencies, and consequences. Lasting security will come from disciplined engineering, continuous verification, and clear responsibility, supported by people who understand how complex systems fail and know how to question the assumptions behind them.

    Related:Microsoft's AI Risk Report Misses This Key Detail

    That hacker mindset has served the industry well, and we need to keep teaching it to developers, defenders, and the next generation of security researchers. The tools and architectures will continue to change, while our responsibility to build systems worthy of trust will endure.

    Related:PapRAT Cyber-Espionage Campaign Leaves a 'Bitter' Taste in South Asia

    Founder and Chief Security Evangelist, Veracode

    Chris Wysopal is the Chief Security Evangelist at Veracode, responsible for enhancing the company’s industry presence, advocating robust security practices, and fostering customer and peer relationships. Prior to co-founding Veracode in 2006, Chris was vice president of research and development at security consultancy @stake, which was acquired by Symantec. In the 1990s, Chris was one of the original vulnerability researchers at The L0pht, a hacker think tank, where he was one of the first to publicize the risks of insecure software. He has testified to the US Congress on the subjects of government security and how vulnerabilities are discovered in software.

    #10502. Sentence Transformers is joining Hugging Face!

    Today, we are announcing that Sentence Transformers is transitioning from Iryna Gurevych’s Ubiquitous Knowledge Processing (UKP) Lab at the TU Darmstadt to Hugging Face. Hugging Face's Tom Aarsen has already been maintaining the library since late 2023 and will continue to lead the project. At its new home, Sentence Transformers will benefit from Hugging Face's robust infrastructure, including continuous integration and testing, ensuring that it stays up-to-date with the latest advancements in Information Retrieval and Natural Language Processing.

    Sentence Transformers (a.k.a. SentenceBERT or SBERT) is a popular open-source library for generating high-quality embeddings that capture semantic meaning. Since its inception by Nils Reimers in 2019, Sentence Transformers has been widely adopted by researchers and practitioners for various natural language processing (NLP) tasks, including semantic search, semantic textual similarity, clustering, and paraphrase mining. After years of development and training by and for the community, over 16,000 Sentence Transformers models are publicly available on the Hugging Face Hub, serving more than a million monthly unique users.

    "Sentence Transformers has been a huge success story and a culmination of our long-standing research on computing semantic similarities for the whole lab. Nils Reimers has made a very timely discovery and has produced not only outstanding research outcomes, but also a highly usable tool. This continues to impact generations of students and practitioners in natural language processing and AI. I would also like to thank all the users and especially the contributors, without whom this project would not be what it is today. And finally, I would like to thank Tom and Hugging Face for taking the project into the future."

    "We're thrilled to officially welcome Sentence Transformers into the Hugging Face family! Over the past two years, it’s been amazing to see this project grow to massive global adoption, thanks to the incredible foundation from the UKP Lab and the amazing community around it. This is just the beginning: we’ll keep doubling down on supporting its growth and innovation, while staying true to the open, collaborative spirit that made it thrive in the first place."

    Sentence Transformers will remain a community-driven, open-source project, with the same open-source license (Apache 2.0) as before. Contributions from researchers, developers, and enthusiasts are welcome and encouraged. The project will continue to prioritize transparency, collaboration, and broad accessibility.

    The Sentence Transformers library was introduced in 2019 by Dr. Nils Reimers at the Ubiquitous Knowledge Processing (UKP) Lab at Technische Universität Darmstadt, under the supervision of Prof. Dr. Iryna Gurevych. Motivated by the limitations of standard BERT embeddings for sentence-level semantic tasks, Sentence-BERT used a Siamese network architecture to produce semantically meaningful sentence embeddings that could be efficiently compared using cosine similarity. Thanks to its modular, open-source design and strong empirical performance on tasks such as semantic textual similarity, clustering, and information retrieval, the library quickly became a staple in the NLP research toolkit, spawning a range of follow-up work and real-world applications that rely on high-quality sentence representations.

    In 2020, multilingual support was added to the library, extending sentence embeddings to more than 400 languages. In 2021, with contributions from Nandan Thakur and Dr. Johannes Daxenberger, the library expanded to support pair-wise sentence scoring using Cross Encoder and Sentence Transformer models. Sentence Transformers was also integrated with the Hugging Face Hub (v2.0). For over four years, the UKP Lab team maintained the library as a community-driven open-source project and provided continued research-driven innovation. During this period, the project's development was supported by grants to Prof. Gurevych by the German Research Foundation (DFG), German Federal Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF), and Hessen State Ministry for Higher Education, Research and the Arts (HMWK).

    In late 2023, Tom Aarsen from Hugging Face took over maintainership of the library, introducing modernized training for Sentence Transformer models (v3.0), as well as improvements of Cross Encoder (v4.0) and Sparse Encoder (v5.0) models.

    The Ubiquitous Knowledge Processing (UKP) Lab at Technische Universität Darmstadt, led by Prof. Dr. Iryna Gurevych, is internationally recognized for its research in natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning. The lab has a long track record of pioneering work in representation learning, large language models, and information retrieval, with numerous publications at leading conferences and journals. Beyond Sentence Transformers, the UKP Lab has developed a number of widely used datasets, benchmarks, and open-source tools that support both academic research and real-world applications.

    Hugging Face would like to thank the UKP Lab and all past and present contributors, especially Dr. Nils Reimers and Prof. Dr. Iryna Gurevych, for their dedication to the project and for entrusting us with its maintenance and now stewardship. We also extend our gratitude to the community of researchers, developers, and practitioners who have contributed to the library's success through model contributions, bug reports, feature requests, documentation improvements, and real-world applications. We are excited to continue building on the strong foundation laid by the UKP Lab and to work with the community to further advance the capabilities of Sentence Transformers.

    Leakers have pieced together a playable version of the canceled Portal prequel F-Stop. Most of the assets came from the massive 12-terabyte leak that dropped this August. That didn’t include the game’s source code or map data, but those final pieces apparently hit the Valve Cut Content Discord this week, allowing a nearly complete version to be pieced together, according to Kotaku.

    Some dialog and elements of F-Stop eventually found their way into Portal 2. But it differs dramatically from the mainline Portal games in that it’s built around a camera mechanic that lets you capture an item by taking its picture and place it elsewhere using the resulting Polaroid-like photos. It’s not unlike Viewfinder in that way.

    The game is short, with videos showing off its full campaign all clocking in at under an hour. That’s not terribly surprising, though. F-Stop was developed as part of the “Directed Design Experiments,” which, according to The Half-Life & Portal Encyclopedia, was a three-month period in 2007 when Valve broke into five teams to build new video game experiments.

    #10500. A Practical Workflow for Testing JavaScript Forms Before Deployment

    Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

    Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

    Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

    Web forms are an essential part of many applications. They allow users to register accounts, submit contact requests, update profiles, and complete purchases. However, a form that appears to work correctly during development can still fail when users enter unexpected values, lose their connection, or submit information multiple times.

    Testing forms before deployment helps developers identify these problems early. Instead of relying only on a successful submission, it is useful to test validation, browser behavior, accessibility, and error handling as separate parts of the workflow.

    Before writing tests, define what the form should do from the user's perspective. A registration form, for example, might require a valid email address, a password that meets specific rules, and confirmation that the user has accepted the terms.

    List the expected outcomes for each field. Consider valid input, empty values, incorrect formats, and unusually long entries. This gives you a clear checklist for testing the form without depending on assumptions about how users will interact with it.

    It is also worth considering what happens after submission. Does the form display a confirmation message? Are users informed when something goes wrong? Can they correct their input without entering everything again?

    These details help establish the expected behavior before testing begins.

    HTML provides several built-in attributes that handle common validation requirements. The required attribute prevents submission when a mandatory field is empty, while type="email" checks whether an email address follows an accepted format.

    This approach reduces the amount of JavaScript needed for basic validation. It also provides a useful starting point for testing browser behavior.

    However, client-side validation should not be treated as a security measure. Users can bypass browser checks, so the server must validate submitted data independently before processing or storing it.

    Developers can also explore SitePoint's HTML and responsive web design guide to understand how form elements fit into layouts across different screen sizes.

    JavaScript becomes useful when a form requires custom rules or more detailed feedback. For example, a password field might need to meet a minimum length, or two fields might need to contain matching values.

    When testing this logic, check both successful and unsuccessful cases. A common mistake is to test only valid submissions, leaving error conditions unexamined.

    Make sure that error messages explain what users need to change. A message such as "Please enter a valid email address" is more useful than a generic notification stating that the submission failed.

    Also check that validation does not unexpectedly clear fields or prevent users from correcting mistakes. Error messages should be associated with the relevant inputs so that keyboard and assistive technology users can identify the problem.

    Browser developer tools help identify problems that are not immediately visible in the interface. The Console panel can reveal JavaScript errors, while the Network panel helps developers inspect requests sent when a form is submitted.

    For example, a form might display a loading indicator but never show a result because its API request returns an error. Inspecting the request status, response, and timing can help distinguish a frontend problem from a backend failure.

    The MDN guide to browser developer tools explains how to inspect page elements, debug JavaScript, and investigate browser behavior.

    Test situations such as an unavailable server, a delayed response, and invalid server-side data. The interface should communicate the problem clearly and provide a reasonable next step.

    A form should remain usable across different devices and input methods. Test it with a keyboard to confirm that users can move between fields, activate buttons, and identify validation errors without a mouse.

    Every input should have a clear label. Placeholder text alone is not a reliable replacement because it disappears when users begin typing.

    Next, test the form at several viewport widths. Check that labels remain readable, buttons are accessible, and fields do not extend beyond their containers. Long error messages should not overlap other elements or break the page layout.

    Automated accessibility checks can identify some issues, but manual testing is still important for understanding the actual user experience.

    A simple checklist makes form testing more consistent across projects:

    Check server errors and slow network responses.

    Confirm that repeated submissions are handled appropriately.

    Test keyboard navigation and accessible error messages.

    Verify the layout on mobile and desktop screens.

    For larger applications, these checks can be supplemented with automated unit and integration tests. Automation is particularly useful when the same validation rules must work consistently across multiple forms.

    Reliable form testing involves more than confirming that a submit button works. Developers need to consider validation, server responses, accessibility, responsive layouts, and unexpected user behavior.

    By combining HTML validation, targeted JavaScript tests, browser developer tools, and a repeatable checklist, teams can identify problems before deployment. The result is a more dependable interface that helps users complete tasks without unnecessary confusion or frustration.

    #10499. Google announces Gemini 4 Carbon with ‘significant gains across coding and agentic tasks’

    Following the launch of Argon two weeks ago, Google today announced Gemini 4 Carbon as its next frontier model.

    There are “significant gains” in coding, agentic tasks, and cybersecurity defense (finding vulnerabilities). Notably, “Carbon ranks #1 on the recently updated v5.0 of Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 59.”

    Google says this fast release is due to its researchers and models “working hand in hand to advance capabilities faster.”

    Based on user feedback following the last launch, Google worked to improve Carbon across “coding, agentic, and scientific tasks, as well as full-stack web development and multimodal understanding.”

    On the safety front, Google worked to improve alignment and trained Carbon to “respond to complex or high-pressure tasks in the right way.”

    Officially, Gemini 4 Carbon is “coming soon to developers, businesses, and consumers.” The model will first be available to “cyber defenders” this week.
