    Stolen Gmail receipts and food-delivery orders feed an AI request for a ‘target assessment’ of each victim.

    When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

    A self-deleting Windows infostealer that calls itself VOLTA-AUTODOXER steals everything it can from a victim’s PC, then asks an AI model, Anthropic’s Claude by default, to turn the haul into a target assessment, Cisco’s Talos research organization reports. The malware builds a structured “evidence bundle” on the person and asks the model for a list of their valuables ranked by how much they could be cashed out for, to see what’s worth the effort. VOLTA operates with a prompt to act as “a forensic intelligence analyst” and to be “blunt, specific, accurate,” and can switch models if one refuses, or even do without.

    It also engages in live enrichment with any stolen sessions. VOLTA searches the victim’s Gmail for receipts from Amazon, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Walmart, and PayPal to confirm a home address, pulls Uber Eats and DoorDash order histories, reuses the stolen Discord token to fill in the victim’s profile, and values Roblox items through Rolimons. The theft list is relatively standard for a stealer, but this enrichment pass turns passive data into something dangerous.

    The data is first assembled locally as Identity_Report.txt and serialized to JSON, before being POSTed to OpenRouter, a popular model router, with the system prompt. Any reply is saved as AI_Analysis.txt, and both are exfiltrated together in a volta_dox.zip archive file. This inference call happens over the victim’s own network connection. The model call asks for a concise assessment of the victim’s suitability as a target, backed by citations, with “opsec” to analyze overall security posture, including password hygiene.

    The settings in use include Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.6 by default, an older model released in February, at a temperature of 0.2. Temperature controls how random a model’s output is from a baseline 1.0, and the hardcoded low value suggests the operator prioritizes predictability. The author likely anticipates refusals, and VOLTA looks for refusal phrases and thin replies, switching to two other models, Moonshot AI’s Kimi K2 and Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash, in that order. If the VOLTA user supplies no API key for OpenRouter, it can still send the dossier over Telegram without the AI data.

    VOLTA appears to be a product designed for resale, as it has a template with six swappable slots — for a custom Telegram channel, API keys, and settings — that are filled at build time. The customer would supply the values, and a custom binary would be created. While the slot credentials are encrypted, it’s possible to recover them from the file. Assuming everything goes to plan with the delivered build, the customer receives ranked target assessments in their Telegram inbox without relying on any attacker-owned infrastructure; the chokepoints are on the services.

    Much of the token theft relies on bypassing Chrome’s App-Bound Encryption (ABE), which VOLTA does by launching Chrome headless, that is, without a GUI. An application-control policy that limits which processes may launch Chrome headless blocks the ABE decryption path. This reduces exposure to VOLTA’s particular method of attack by denying it access to Chrome-stored sessions, but it doesn’t stop its other theft, the AI stage, or exfiltration.

    Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

    After infection, the main executable may delete itself, but a volta_debug.txt file should be preserved by the victim. This file is a log that shows what was collected and whether the LLM call was successful. The target should revoke or rotate all API keys and tokens and change passwords, regardless of exposure; likewise, any funds in a wallet whose seed phrase was stored in plaintext should be moved to a new wallet with a fresh seed, preferably generated on an air-gapped device.

    One very real concern is that VOLTA’s use of AI is relatively narrow compared with what is possible with fully AI-assisted malware, especially as models could be utilized for additional phases. Refusal resilience may become a standard design requirement for malware as AI integration matures. Already, a Windows malware implant reported in September was built around a panel of up to four LLMs that vote on its next move, and another, reported this week, can fall back to using the victim’s own OpenAI API key. This is still a process of having AI replace the work a human analyst would normally do, so the real question is which stage is next.

    #10436. Risks & Rewards: How AI Is Redefining the CISO's Role

    Nvidia security executive Mark Weatherford says CISOs must help business leaders weigh AI's pros and cons, and ensure those deploying it own the risks.

    ISC2 Strategic Congress 2026 — Denver — The CISO role is evolving around AI, with security leaders now expected to help the business gain a competitive edge with it while also using the technology to help manage cyber-risk.

    Doing both jobs at once means keeping up with technology that changes by the month, Mark Weatherford, Nvidia's head of cybersecurity policy and strategic engagement, said this week at the ISC2 Strategic Congress 2026.

    "Speed is the biggest challenge right now," Weatherford said in a conference session on the evolving CISO role in the AI era. "Technology is changing so fast it is really hard for us to keep pace."

    The shift shows up in routine practices too, he noted. Penetration testing four times a year, for instance, once counted as adequate. Now, anyone not testing around the clock is probably not testing enough.

    Weatherford served as deputy undersecretary for cybersecurity at DHS in the Obama administration and was previously chief information security officer for the state of Colorado and the state of California. His other career highlights include serving as chief security officer of the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) and as a security leader at Booking Holdings.

    Related:As AI Reshapes the SOC Career Ladder, Satisfaction Rises for 91%, but Entry Gets Harder for Nearly Half

    Weatherford pointed to a sense of FOMO — or a fear of missing out — as driving many organizations to deploy AI without always doing business due diligence or understanding what value they might be deriving from their investment. While there are many instances where the rush to spend might make sense, there are other cases where the case for AI may not be as clear-cut.

    CISOs often, though, have the opposite tendency, which is defaulting to "no" when there is the slightest element of risk involved. Weatherford pointed to the Navy concept of command by negation where subordinates take autonomous action to meet an overall goal unless the superior asks them to stop.

    He opined that cybersecurity leaders should similarly be willing to accept more risk on their own, calibrated to their company's risk tolerance. "You have to be curious. You have to be willing to step out of your comfort zone," he said.

    Weatherford encouraged CISOs to continuously think about how AI can help transform business and security and look for opportunities to make themselves better in their role. CISOs who expect their reputations and past work alone to carry them through the future are limiting their potential, he cautioned.

    "Be curious, be creative, be willing to learn and relearn," Weatherford said, adding that one way to get up to speed on AI is to pick up one new topic every week.

    Related:Fighting Your Dragons Through Tough Tech Times

    The worry about being too slow to tap AI comes amid growing concern about organizations moving too quickly to implement AI without considering appropriate controls or without a full appreciation of associated risks, Weatherford noted. It is the role of the CISO to make sure the board understands the risks and knows who owns each risk, especially when another executive's deployment creates it.

    Such frankness can potentially be career-limiting at times, Weatherford conceded. But CISOs often end up getting blamed for decisions that are not theirs, and they need to push back, he advised. "I would say we need to make sure that the people taking the risk are responsible for the risk.

    For the talent pipeline, Weatherford favors paid internships that bring AI-native young people into the company and teach them the business. One of his interview ideas is to hand a candidate a business problem and let them use AI to solve it live, with no single right answer, to test flexibility.

    It's also important for CISOs to ensure that people continue to have a career path and upward mobility within the organization, Weatherford said. It's a mistake to assume that paying people more and keeping them in their same roles is a way to retain talent.

    Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

    Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

    His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

    #10434. Open ASR Leaderboard: Trends and Insights with New Multilingual & Long-Form Tracks

    While everyone (and their grandma 👵) is spinning up new ASR models, picking the right one for your use case can feel more overwhelming than choosing your next Netflix show. As of 21 Nov 2025, there are 150 Audio-Text-to-Text and 27K ASR models on the Hub 🤯

    Most benchmarks focus on short-form English transcription (<30s), and overlook other important tasks, such as (1) multilingual performance and (2) model throughput, which can a be deciding factor for long-form audio like meetings and podcasts.

    Over the past two years, the Open ASR Leaderboard has become a standard for comparing open and closed-source models on both accuracy and efficiency. Recently, multilingual and long-form transcription tracks have been added to the leaderboard 🎉

    As of 21 Nov 2025, the Open ASR Leaderboard compares 60+ open and closed-source models from 18 organizations, across 11 datasets.

    In a recent preprint, we dive into the technical setup and highlight some key trends in modern ASR. Here are the big takeaways 👇

    Models combining Conformer encoders with large language model (LLM) decoders currently lead in English transcription accuracy. For example, NVIDIA’s Canary-Qwen-2.5B, IBM’s Granite-Speech-3.3-8B, and Microsoft’s Phi-4-Multimodal-Instruct achieve the lowest word error rates (WER), showing that integrating LLM reasoning can significantly boost ASR accuracy.

    💡 Pro-tip: NVIDIA introduced Fast Conformer, a 2x faster variant of the Conformer, that is used in their Canary and Parakeet suite of models.

    While highly accurate, these LLM decoders tend to be slower than simpler approaches. On the Open ASR Leaderboard, efficiency is measured using inverse real-time factor (RTFx), where higher is better.

    For even faster inference, CTC and TDT decoders deliver 10–100× faster throughput, albeit with slightly higher error rates. This makes them ideal for real-time, offline, or batch transcription tasks (such as meetings, lectures, or podcasts).

    OpenAI’s Whisper Large v3 remains a strong multilingual baseline, supporting 99 languages. However, fine-tuned or distilled variants like Distil-Whisper and CrisperWhisper often outperform the original on English-only tasks, showing how targeted fine-tuning can improve specialization (how to fine-tune? Check out guides for Whisper, Parakeet, and Voxtral).

    That said, focusing on English tends to reduce multilingual coverage 👉 a classic case of the tradeoff between specialization and generalization. Similarly, while self-supervised systems like Meta’s Massively Multilingual Speech (MMS) and Omnilingual ASR can support 1K+ languages, they trail behind language-specific encoders in accuracy.

    ⭐ While just five languages are currently benchmarked, we’re planning to expand to more languages and are excited for new dataset and models contributions to multilingual ASR through GitHub pull requests.

    🎯 Alongside multilingual benchmarks, several community-driven leaderboards focus on individual languages. For example, the Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard compares models across Modern Standard Arabic and regional dialects, highlighting how speech variation and diglossia challenge current systems. Similarly. the Russian ASR Leaderboard provides a growing hub for evaluating encoder-decoder and CTC models on Russian-specific phonology and morphology. These localized efforts mirror the broader multilingual leaderboard’s mission to encourage dataset sharing, fine-tuned checkpoints, and transparent model comparisons, especially in languages with fewer established ASR resources.

    For long-form audio (e.g., podcasts, lectures, meetings), closed-source systems still edge out open ones. It could be due to domain tuning, custom chunking, or production-grade optimization.

    Among open models, OpenAI’s Whisper Large v3 performs the best. But for throughput, CTC-based Conformers shine 👉 for example, NVIDIA’s Parakeet CTC 1.1B achieves an RTFx of 2793.75, compared to 68.56 for Whisper Large v3, with only a moderate WER degradation (6.68 and 6.43 respectively).

    The tradeoff? Parakeet is English-only, again reminding us of that multilingual and specialization tradeoff 🫠.

    ⭐ While closed systems still lead, there’s huge potential for open-source innovation here. Long-form ASR remains one of the most exciting frontiers for the community to tackle next!

    Given how fast ASR is evolving, we’re excited to see what new architectures push performance and efficiency, and how the Open ASR Leaderboard continues to serve as a transparent, community-driven benchmark for the field, and as a reference for other leaderboards (Russian, Arabic, and Speech DeepFake Detection).

    We’ll keep expanding the Open ASR LeaderBoard with more models, more languages, and more datasets so stay tuned 👀

    👉 Want to contribute? Head on over to the GitHub repo to open a pull request 🚀

    #10433. IQOO’s new mid-range phone puts last year’s flagships to shame

    The IQOO Neo 12 is outfitted with so many premium-level specs that you’d never know this was targeted toward an upper mid-range budget.

    Companies like IQOO often surprise with specs that feel like they shouldn’t belong on relatively inexpensive phones, and the IQOO Neo 12 fits right in with that. The star of the show is the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, the same one in the $1300 Galaxy S26 Ultra. That’s made even better thanks to a custom 59-blade active cooling fan and a “3D Ice Dome” vapor chamber inside.

    On the front is a generous 6.83-inch 185Hz AMOLED panel with 2K resolution, a 2,200-nit peak brightness rate, and both DC dimming and 2,160Hz PWM dimming for eye comfort. Unsurprisingly, for a gaming-centric phone, it’s also got a custom display chip for IQOO 16-level touch responsiveness and a “super-sensitive gyro” for epic gyro aiming in games.

    Despite having an active fan, this one features an IP69 rating, so it can be abused in all sorts of ways without seeing water or dust damage. A 9,000mAh battery is inside with support for 100W wired charging, and an ultrasonic fingerprint sensor, IR sensor, and stereo speakers round out the build.

    The IQOO Neo 12 packs a 50MP Sony IMX921 main camera sensor alongside an 8MP ultra-wide camera in the stylish raised camera island on the back, plus a 16MP selfie up front. Phone colorway options include Contender, Frost Blade Blue, and Shadow Black. This one is making its initial debut in China for:

    Not too shabby, given the specs. Chinese users can buy it from Vivo right now. A global release date has not yet been announced.
